content: 1. Requiring the consent, agreement, or guarantee of a relative to access abortion services constitutes discrimination, as noted in the 2016 report of the United Nations Working Group on the issue of discrimination against women in law and practice (UN Doc. A/HRC/32/44). 2. Barriers to accessing lawful abortion that are not based on medical necessity, such as authorization requirements, are discriminatory, according to the same 2016 UN report. 3. States are obligated to take measures to reduce maternal morbidity and mortality, including addressing unsafe abortions, particularly in settings where challenges are exacerbated. This is emphasized in the CESCR General Comment No. 22 on the right to sexual and reproductive health (Article 12 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, 2016, UN Doc. E/C.12/GC/22). 4. States must ensure that women do not have to resort to life-threatening clandestine abortions. This is highlighted in the HRC General Comment No. 28 on Article 3 (The Equality of Rights between Men and Women, 2000, UN Doc. 10). 5. States are required to liberalize restrictive abortion laws and address barriers such as the criminalization of women who undergo abortions, as stated in CESCR General Comment No. 22 (2016). 6. Laws regulating abortion must not violate women’s and girls’ right to life, jeopardize their lives, subject them to physical or mental suffering, discriminate against them, or arbitrarily interfere with their privacy, as outlined in HRC General Comment No. 36 on Article 6 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (2018, UN Doc. CCPR/C/GC/36). 7. States must provide safe, legal, and effective access to abortion where the life or health of the pregnant woman is at risk, or where carrying a pregnancy to term would cause substantial pain or suffering, such as in cases of rape or non-viable pregnancies (HRC General Comment No. 36, 2018). 8. Abortion and abortion-related healthcare must be available in cases of fatal fetal anomalies, as established in cases such as Whelan v. Ireland (2017) and Mellet v. Ireland (2016). 9. States should allow women to terminate pregnancies on request during the first trimester or later in specific cases, as recommended in the 2016 report of the UN Working Group on discrimination against women in law and practice. 10. Post-abortion care must be confidential and unconditional, and it must not depend on a woman’s willingness to cooperate with any subsequent criminal investigation. This is emphasized in the Special Rapporteur’s Interim Report to the General Assembly (2011, UN Doc. A/66/254). 11. Post-abortion care must not be used as evidence in legal proceedings against women or abortion care providers, as stated in the same 2011 report by the Special Rapporteur. 12. States must repeal laws and regulations that impede rural women’s access to sexual and reproductive health services, including those criminalizing abortion, requiring mandatory waiting periods, or necessitating third-party consent for abortion (CEDAW General Recommendation No. 34, 2016). 13. Adolescent sexual and reproductive health services, including safe abortion care, must be confidential and non-judgmental, as highlighted in the Special Rapporteur’s 2016 report to the General Assembly (UN Doc. A/HRC/32/32). 14. States must ensure that measures regulating abortion are evidence-based and proportionate, and they must not perpetuate unsafe conditions or violate the right to health, as emphasized in the Special Rapporteur’s Interim Report to the General Assembly (2011). 15. Requiring judicial authorization for abortion violates the right to privacy, as it involves judicial intervention in matters that should be resolved between the patient and physician. This requirement often leads to illegal abortions, as noted in the case of LMR v. Argentina (2011, UN Doc. CCPR/C/101/D/1608/2007). 16. States must remove existing barriers and refrain from implementing new ones that deny women and girls effective access to safe abortion services, as stated in HRC General Comment No. 36 (2018). 17. The deliberate denial of life-saving medical care due to a legal ban on abortion constitutes a violation of the right to life and may amount to a gender-based arbitrary killing, as noted in the Special Rapporteur’s 2017 report on extrajudicial, summary, or arbitrary executions (UN Doc. A/HRC/35/23).
